clinicalPearls: A thrombotic microangiopathy defined by the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury
The typical form follows a Shiga-toxin-producing enteric infection (often E. coli O157:H7), classically preceded by bloody diarrhoea, and predominantly affects children
Atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the alternative complement pathway, is often familial, and tends to relapse and progress to end-stage renal disease
The blood film shows fragmented red cells (schistocytes) with a raised LDH, low haptoglobin, and a negative direct antiglobulin test, indicating mechanical (non-immune) haemolysis
Renal involvement dominates the clinical picture, distinguishing HUS from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, in which neurological features and severe ADAMTS13 deficiency predominate
Measuring ADAMTS13 activity helps separate TTP (severely reduced) from HUS (usually normal or only modestly reduced), which is critical because treatments differ
Shiga-toxin-associated HUS is largely managed with meticulous supportive care and dialysis when needed, and antibiotics are generally avoided as they may worsen toxin release
Complement-mediated atypical HUS responds to terminal complement blockade, which has substantially improved renal and overall outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy in which endothelial injury triggers platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels, especially the renal microvasculature. In Shiga-toxin-associated disease, toxin absorbed from the gut binds glomerular and endothelial cells, causing injury, platelet activation, and microvascular thrombosis. In atypical HUS, uncontrolled activation of the alternative complement pathway, from inherited or acquired defects in complement regulatory proteins, drives endothelial damage. The resulting microthrombi mechanically shear passing red cells (producing schistocytes and haemolysis), consume platelets (causing thrombocytopenia), and obstruct renal perfusion (causing acute kidney injury).
additionalDifferentials: Systemic vasculitis or scleroderma renal crisis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for schistocytes and thrombocytopenia
Haemolysis markers: LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, and a direct antiglobulin test (expected negative)
Renal function, urinalysis, and monitoring of urine output
Stool testing and culture for Shiga-toxin-producing organisms
ADAMTS13 activity to exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
Complement studies and genetic testing for regulatory protein defects in suspected atypical HUS
redFlags: Rapidly progressive acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria requiring urgent dialysis
Neurological deterioration raising concern for overlapping TTP or CNS involvement
Hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, or refractory hypertension as life-threatening complications of renal failure
reference.prognosis: Shiga-toxin-associated HUS in children often recovers with supportive care, though a minority sustain chronic kidney damage; atypical, complement-mediated HUS historically carried a high risk of end-stage renal disease and death, but outcomes have improved markedly with complement-blocking therapy.
pitfalls: Confusing HUS with TTP and delaying the correct treatment; ADAMTS13 testing helps distinguish them
Giving antibiotics in Shiga-toxin-associated HUS, which may increase toxin release and worsen disease
Attributing thrombocytopenia and anaemia to sepsis or DIC without examining the film for schistocytes
Failing to consider atypical HUS in relapsing or familial disease and missing the opportunity for complement inhibition
Transfusing platelets reflexively, which can aggravate microvascular thrombosis
management: In diarrhoea-associated (Shiga-toxin) disease, give supportive care alone and avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents, which may worsen toxin release

In atypical, complement-mediated disease, initiate terminal complement blockade with a C5-inhibiting monoclonal antibody such as eculizumab, with meningococcal vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis before treatment
Commence plasma exchange empirically when thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura cannot yet be excluded, pending ADAMTS13 results
Provide supportive care with careful fluid and electrolyte correction, control of hypertension, and transfusion of red cells for symptomatic anaemia
Institute renal replacement therapy for oliguric acute kidney injury, fluid overload, or refractory electrolyte disturbance
Monitor haemolysis markers, platelet count, and renal function to track response and detect relapse
Refer to nephrology and haematology, and arrange complement genetic testing with family screening and counselling in atypical disease
